newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper urges progress in troop release.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper urges progress in troop release.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper is calling for less publicity and more progress in efforts to free 60 Colombian troops held prisoner by leftist rebels for more than two months.

In interviews with Colombian media during the Ibero-American summit, which ended on Monday, Samper criticised the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), the country's largest and oldest guerrilla force, for using the soldiers' release for political propaganda purposes.

Meanwhile, army commanders played down growing rumours, fuelled by an anonymous statement sent to some media in recent days, that 30 of the 60 soldiers, seized by the FARC in southern Colombia on Aug. 30, may now be dead.

"This situation is not the time for armed or political propaganda. I have met with heads of the International Committee of the Red Cross and asked them to concentrate efforts on the release of the soldiers in a way that there is less publicity and more progress," Samper told TV news.

The capture of the 60 soldiers from the Las Delicias base, in a jungle region of southern Putumayo province, signalled the start of one of the bloodiest guerrilla offensives in more than three decades of armed uprising.

The attack was a humiliating blow to the army and, according to political analysts, its sense of dishonour is being compounded by the FARC's demands to hand over the troops to an international mediation committee.

Despite the FARC's call for large swathes of southern Caqueta province to be demilitarized for the eventual release of its prisoners, thousands of extra troops have been drafted into the area and government officials have said that military operations will continue until a handover date is set.
The FARC has accused the military of planning to save face and rescue the soldiers by force even if it means that some die in the attempt -- claims denied by the army.
Over the weekend some local media have received anonymous statements claiming that as many as 30 of the 60 prisoners may have died, the Caracol radio network reported.

In comments to the radio station on Monday, a regional army commander in southern Colombia, Gen. Nestor Ramirez, said the unsourced statements should be ignored, adding that the senders could be trying to inflame an already delicate situation.

Rumours that some of the soldiers may have died from jungle diseases and wounds sustained in the original attacks are not new but have so far been denied by the FARC. Spokesmen for the FARC could not be contacted for comments on the latest claims.
